title: The Instructional Hierarchy and EBLI: A Fitting Pair
author: Elana Gordon
summary: Elana Gordon, a teacher using a linguistic phonics approach called Evidence-Based Literacy Instruction (EBLI), responds to a conference claim that only print-to-speech phonics follows the instructional hierarchy and that anything else harms children. She walks through the four stages of Haring and colleagues' framework (acquisition, fluency, generalization and adaptation) and shows how EBLI routines map onto each. Sound sorts with explicit instruction and immediate feedback serve acquisition, multisyllabic reading and spelling routines build fluency, and Read, Read Back, Read Again supports generalization with authentic texts. Adaptation comes from using the routines across the day so scaffolds can be removed. She concludes that linguistic phonics follows the hierarchy and has accelerated growth for her students. She cautions against condemning approaches, citing Tim Shanahan's point that the two approaches have not been compared side by side.
points: The instructional hierarchy describes a continuum from acquisition to fluency, generalization and adaptation, and can be used to judge whether an approach is sound.
In acquisition, EBLI sound sorts use explicit teaching with immediate feedback at every step.
Multisyllabic reading and spelling routines build fluency by integrating many phoneme-grapheme associations.
Read, Read Back, Read Again moves students into authentic texts to generalize, and daily use of the routines supports adaptation.
Claims that one phonics direction is harmful go beyond the evidence, since print-to-speech and speech-to-print have not been studied side by side.
quotes: The instructional hierarchy is a framework developed by Haring et al. (1978). It demonstrates a continuum that learners fall into as they begin to acquire and develop skills.
During a conference session I attended last year, it was implied that only print-to-speech phonics instruction followed the instructional hierarchy. Anything else was hurting children.
Learners in this stage are initially learning a particular skill. They may be inaccurate and laborious in their performance.

This particular strategy also provides mixed practice for students because every time a multisyllabic word is read, students integrate the reading and spelling of many phoneme/grapheme associations they have learned.
Students often can read words in isolation or in decodable texts accurately but perform inaccurately or less fluently in new contexts.

EBLI is not a time of day for these students; it is an innate way of reading and writing that is integrated across all domains of language. Because of this approach, students can adapt their learning and internalize it.
These two approaches have not been studied side-by-side; therefore, the claim that one is “harming” children cannot be made.
